title: Your Antidepressant Isn't Working: What to Do Next
description: When medication doesn't help depression or anxiety. Possible reasons, what to try next, and options for treatment-resistant depression.

content.text: You've been on medication for weeks. Nothing's changed—or maybe you feel worse. Here's what to consider and what to try next.
Have You Given It Enough Time?

items: Most antidepressants take 4-8 weeks for full effect
Some improvement should appear by week 2-4
If zero improvement by week 6-8, it's probably not working

content.text: Many people are on subtherapeutic doses. Starting doses are often not treatment doses. Ask your doctor if there's room to increase.
Missing doses regularly significantly reduces effectiveness.

items: Wrong medication for your depression subtype
Metabolic differences (some people metabolize drugs faster)
Misdiagnosis (e.g., bipolar depression responds differently)
Substance use interfering
Untreated medical conditions (thyroid, sleep apnea)
Severe life stressors overwhelming medication effects
Increase dose if possible
Ensure consistent timing and adherence
Address factors that interfere (alcohol, other drugs)
Try different SSRI (different people respond to different ones)
Try different class (SNRI, bupropion, mirtazapine)
Each medication has 50-60% response rate—failure of one doesn't predict failure of others
Add second medication to boost first (aripiprazole, lithium, thyroid)
Add therapy if not already doing it
This approach often helps when switching alone doesn't

content.text: If you've tried 2+ medications without adequate response:

items: Spravato (esketamine) - FDA approved for treatment-resistant depression
TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation)
ECT (electroconvulsive therapy) - most effective for severe cases
Ketamine infusions
Clinical trials for novel treatments

content.text: Treatment-resistant depression is treatable. Options exist beyond standard antidepressants. Don't give up.

items: 'Am I on an adequate dose?'
'Should we try a different medication or class?'
'Should we add something to what I'm taking?'
'Could this be something other than depression?'
'Should I see a psychiatrist?' (if you're seeing a PCP)
'Are there other options like TMS or ketamine?'

content.text: One medication not working doesn't mean nothing will. Most people find something that helps—it just takes trial and error. Stay in communication with your prescriber, consider adding therapy, and know that advanced options exist for treatment-resistant cases.
